los.text: Describe the main causes, signs, symptoms and investigations of common causes of potential spinal cord damage
los.html:
Causes
  • Trauma (RTA, falls, sport)
  • Compression (metastatic spinal cord compression: breast, lung, prostate, renal, myeloma; disc prolapse; epidural abscess/haematoma; cervical spondylotic myelopathy)
  • Vascular (anterior spinal artery infarct, AV malformation)
  • Inflammatory/demyelinating (MS, transverse myelitis, NMO)
  • Infection (TB/Pott's, HIV, syphilis, HTLV-1)
  • Metabolic (B12 deficiency → subacute combined degeneration, copper deficiency, nitrous oxide abuse)
  • Degenerative (MND)
  • Tumours (intrinsic: ependymoma, astrocytoma)
  • Syringomyelia.
Symptoms/signs
  • Back/neck pain (radicular band-like pain), limb weakness (often legs), sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction (retention, incontinence), sexual dysfunction.
  • UMN signs below lesion (spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars; acutely may be flaccid = spinal shock)
  • LMN signs at level of lesion.
Cord syndromes
  • Complete transection
  • Brown-Séquard (hemisection: ipsilateral weakness + dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss)
  • Anterior cord (motor + spinothalamic loss, dorsal columns spared)
  • Central cord (arms > legs; hyperextension in elderly)
  • Cauda equina (LMN: saddle anaesthesia, retention/incontinence, bilateral sciatica).
Ix
  • Urgent whole-spine MRI (within 24 h for suspected MSCC, immediately if neurological deficit)
  • Bloods (FBC, CRP/ESR, Ca²⁺, B12/folate, myeloma screen, PSA)
  • CT for trauma
  • LP/CSF for inflammatory/infective
  • Bladder scan (post-void residual).
Back pain + neurology in a cancer patient = MSCC: dexamethasone 16 mg, urgent MRI, oncology/spinal surgery referral.

los.text: Describe the clinical assessment of an individual presenting with weak legs (considering time frame and clinical signs), investigations, differential diagnosis and treatment principles (spinal cord stroke; acute and chronic spinal cord compression; motor neuron disease)
los.html:
History
  • Time course is key: sudden (minutes: vascular/spinal stroke, trauma, haematoma), acute/subacute (hours–days: cord compression from metastases/abscess, GBS, transverse myelitis), chronic progressive (months: cervical myelopathy, MND, tumour, B12, hereditary spastic paraparesis).
  • Pain, sensory symptoms, bladder/bowel, cancer history, fever/IVDU, systemic features.
Examination
  • UMN vs LMN signs
  • Sensory level (cord) vs glove-and-stocking (neuropathy) vs saddle (cauda equina)
  • Pure motor (MND, myopathy, NMJ)
  • Fasciculations
  • Cranial nerves (bulbar = MND, brainstem)
  • Spinal tenderness
  • PR/anal tone.
CauseKey featuresManagement
Spinal cord stroke (anterior spinal artery)Sudden pain + paraplegia, loss of pain/temperature, preserved proprioception/vibration; aortic surgery/dissectionSupportive, treat cause, antiplatelet, rehab
Acute cord compression (MSCC, abscess, haematoma, disc)Back pain → weakness, sensory level, sphincter disturbance over hours–daysEmergency MRI, dexamethasone (MSCC), radiotherapy/surgical decompression, antibiotics + drainage (abscess)
Chronic compression (cervical spondylotic myelopathy)Elderly; clumsy hands, gait unsteadiness, neck stiffness, mixed UMN (legs) + LMN (arms)MRI; surgical decompression if progressive
MND (ALS commonest)Progressive painless weakness, mixed UMN + LMN signs, fasciculations, bulbar palsy; no sensory loss, sphincters spared, eye movements sparedEMG; riluzole (modest survival), NIV, gastrostomy (PEG/RIG), MDT, palliative care
Peripheral differentialsGBS (areflexia, ascending), myopathy (proximal), myasthenia (fatigable)NCS/EMG, CK, antibodies

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis and principles of management of multiple sclerosis
los.html:
Pathophysiology
  • Autoimmune demyelination of CNS (oligodendrocytes/myelin) by autoreactive T cells (Th1/Th17) and B cells crossing BBB → plaques of demyelination
  • Inflammation
  • Gliosis
  • and axonal loss (drives permanent disability).
  • Lesions "disseminated in space and time"
  • Typical sites: periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial (brainstem/cerebellum), spinal cord, optic nerve.
  • Risk: female (3:1), age 20–40, northern latitude (↓ vitamin D), EBV, smoking, HLA-DRB1*15:01.
Clinical
  • Optic neuritis (painful visual loss, ↓ colour vision, RAPD)
  • Sensory symptoms
  • Limb weakness/spasticity
  • Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
  • Diplopia
  • Cerebellar ataxia
  • Bladder (urgency)
  • Fatigue
  • Depression
  • Cognitive impairment
  • Lhermitte's sign (electric shock on neck flexion)
  • Uhthoff's phenomenon (worse with heat).
TypesClinically isolated syndrome → relapsing–remitting (~85%) → secondary progressive; primary progressive (~10–15%).
Diagnosis (McDonald criteria)
  • Clinical + MRI (T2/FLAIR white matter lesions, gadolinium-enhancing = active) showing dissemination in space and time
  • CSF oligoclonal bands (unmatched in serum) can substitute for dissemination in time
  • Visual evoked potentials.
  • Exclude mimics (B12, NMO: AQP4 antibodies, MOGAD, sarcoid).
Management
  • Relapse: high-dose methylprednisolone (oral or IV, 3–5 days) → speeds recovery, doesn't change long-term outcome.
  • Disease-modifying therapies (reduce relapses): moderate (interferon-β, glatiramer, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide), high efficacy (natalizumab (PML risk), ocrelizumab (anti-CD20; also PPMS), alemtuzumab, cladribine, S1P modulators like fingolimod), autologous HSCT.
  • Symptomatic: spasticity (baclofen, gabapentin, tizanidine, physio), bladder (antimuscarinics, intermittent self-catheterisation), fatigue (amantadine, exercise), neuropathic pain, depression; MDT (MS nurse, OT, physio); vitamin D, smoking cessation.

los.text: Explain the role of the central nervous system in determining the relationship between afferent nerve activity and perceived sensation (include higher cortical dysfunction)
los.html:
Sensory transduction
  • Receptors convert stimuli into receptor potentials → APs.
  • Coding: intensity by firing frequency and recruitment
  • Modality by labelled line (specific receptor and pathway)
  • Location by receptive field and somatotopic map (homunculus).
  • Adaptation: rapidly adapting (Pacinian, Meissner: vibration, touch) vs slowly adapting (Merkel, Ruffini: pressure, stretch).
Pathways(three-neuron chains → contralateral cortex)
  • Dorsal column–medial lemniscus: fine touch, vibration, proprioception; ascends ipsilaterally → decussates in medulla (internal arcuate fibres) → VPL thalamus → primary somatosensory cortex (S1, postcentral gyrus).
  • Spinothalamic (anterolateral): pain, temperature, crude touch; decussates in spinal cord within 1–2 segments → VPL thalamus → S1 (+ limbic/insular for affective pain).
  • Spinocerebellar tracts: unconscious proprioception.
Perception is modified centrally
  • Gate control theory (Melzack & Wall: Aβ touch fibres inhibit pain transmission in dorsal horn)
  • Descending inhibition (periaqueductal grey → rostral ventromedial medulla; endogenous opioids, 5-HT, NA)
  • Central sensitisation (chronic pain)
  • Attention
  • Emotion
  • Expectation (placebo).
Higher cortical functionS1 (discrimination) → association cortex (parietal: integration, body image, spatial awareness).
Higher cortical dysfunction (parietal lobe)
  • Astereognosis (can't identify objects by touch)
  • Agraphaesthesia
  • Loss of 2-point discrimination
  • Sensory inattention/extinction
  • Neglect (usually left-sided neglect from right parietal lesion)
  • Agnosias (visual agnosia, prosopagnosia: temporal/occipital)
  • Anosognosia
  • Gerstmann syndrome (dominant parietal: acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, left–right confusion).

los.text: Describe the neural pathways involved in the control of voluntary movement (pyramidal system, basal nuclei, cerebellum), and how damage to these pathways influence controlled movement
los.html:
Pyramidal (corticospinal) system
  • Primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus; somatotopic homunculus)
  • → internal capsule (posterior limb)
  • → cerebral peduncle
  • → pons
  • → medullary pyramids
  • → ~85–90% decussate
  • → lateral corticospinal tract
  • → anterior horn cells (LMN)
  • → muscle.
  • Corticobulbar fibres to cranial nerve nuclei (mostly bilateral; except lower face and CN XII).
UMN lesion
  • Weakness in pyramidal pattern (extensors of arms, flexors of legs), spasticity (clasp-knife), hyperreflexia, clonus, upgoing plantar (Babinski), no wasting early.
  • Acute: initially flaccid.
  • Lesion above decussation → contralateral signs.
LMN lesionWeakness, wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia, ↓/absent reflexes, downgoing plantars.
Basal ganglia(caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra)
  • Modulate movement via direct (facilitates movement) and indirect (inhibits) pathways through thalamus to cortex
  • Dopamine from substantia nigra pars compacta (D1 excites direct, D2 inhibits indirect).
  • Lesions → hypokinetic (Parkinson's: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor) or hyperkinetic (Huntington's chorea, hemiballismus from contralateral subthalamic nucleus lesion, dystonia).
Cerebellum
  • Compares intended vs actual movement (input: spinocerebellar, vestibular, pontine; output via deep nuclei → thalamus → cortex) → coordination, balance, motor learning.
  • Ipsilateral signs: "DANISH": Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia (gait/limb), Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Slurred/scanning Speech, Hypotonia (+ past-pointing, heel–shin).
  • Vermis lesions → truncal ataxia
  • Hemisphere lesions → limb ataxia.
